turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I ask for no explanation of what he told me. I perfectly well believe every thing that he said. I perfectly well know that you have employed him in every kind of dishonesty.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Your convictions are strong and your prejudices are equally so. But I have never employed Mr. Wickham in dishonesty, nor have I ever acted in a manner to deserve your accusations.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: I have no doubt of your integrity, Mr. Darcy, but your actions speak louder than your words. I have seen the consequences of your choices and they have not been kind to those around you.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your perceptions are clouded by prejudice and misunderstanding. I have done nothing to warrant such harsh accusations and it pains me to see you so misinformed.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your words may be sincere, but they do little to change the reality of the situation. I must admit, it is difficult for me to overlook the evidence of your past actions.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: I am aware that my actions have been misconstrued, Miss Bennet, but I assure you that my intentions have always been honorable, regardless of how they may have appeared to you.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your assurance does little to alter the fact that I have observed your actions and their effects. It is not my intention to misjudge you, but the evidence is clear and hard to ignore.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, if you would give me the opportunity to explain, I believe I could alleviate your misconceptions and perhaps earn a portion of your goodwill.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I appreciate your confidence in your own character, but I cannot dismiss the impact of your actions on others, especially those closest to me.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I understand the difficulty of your position, but I implore you to consider the possibility that there is more to my character than what you have seen.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your words are kind, but my feelings towards you are deeply rooted in the pain caused by your actions. It will take more than words to change that.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I am aware of the depth of your feelings, and I do not expect them to change overnight. My hope is that as time passes, you will come to see me in a different light.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, your hope is your own to hold. I must be true to my own feelings and the experiences that have shaped them. I wish you well, but I cannot alter my opinion.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your candor is as sharp as ever. I shall respect your feelings and give you the time and space to reconsider our acquaintance.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I appreciate your respect for my feelings. I hope that you may find happiness in your own path.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your words are not unexpected. I shall indeed seek my own happiness and leave you to yours.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, I wish you every success and happiness in your endeavors.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, I shall respect your wishes and withdraw from your presence.

turns.speaker: Elizabeth
turns.text: Mr. Darcy, before you go, I must confess that despite my dislike, I have been struck by your sincerity and depth of feeling.

turns.speaker: Mr. Darcy
turns.text: Miss Bennet, your candor is as much a part of your character as your fairness of mind. I am at a loss for words.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: In such cases as this, it is, I believe, the established mode to express a sense of obligation for the sentiments avowed, however unequally they may be returned. It is natural that obligation should be felt, and if I could feel gratitude, I would now thank you. But I cannot--I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly. I am sorry to have occasioned pain to anyone. It has been most unconsciously done, however, and I hope will be of short duration. The feelings which you tell me have long prevented the acknowledgment of your regard can have little difficulty in overcoming it after this explanation.

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: And this is all the reply which I am to have the honour of expecting! I might, perhaps, wish to be informed why, with so little endeavour at civility, I am thus rejected. But it is of small importance.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I might as well inquire, why, with so evident a design of offending and insulting me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character? Was not this some excuse for incivility, if I was uncivil? But I have other provocations. You know I have. Had not my own feelings decided against you, had they been indifferent, or had they even been favourable, do you think that any consideration would tempt me to accept the man who has been the means of ruining, perhaps for ever, the happiness of a most beloved sister?

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: I have every reason in the world to think ill of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you acted there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you have been the principal, if not the only means of dividing them from each other, of exposing one to the censure of the world for caprice and instability, the other to its derision for disappointed hopes, and involving them both in misery of the acutest kind.

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: But it is not merely this affair, on which my dislike is founded. Long before it had taken place, my opinion of you was decided. Your character was unfolded in the recital which I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On this subject, what can you have to say? In what imaginary act of friendship can you here defend yourself? or under what misrepresentation can you here impose upon others?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: You take an eager interest in that gentleman’s concerns

opening.speaker: Elizabeth
opening.text: Who that knows what his misfortunes have been can help feeling an interest in him?

opening.speaker: Mr. Darcy
opening.text: His misfortunes! yes, his misfortunes have been great indeed.
